portion_doctrine: Gary Vee talk on modern marketing (2026 corporate presentation + podcast interview segment). Core thesis: shift from traditional media buying to 'midfunnel' organic social strategy. Interest-media (algorithm-driven, relevance-based) beats follower-counting social media. Emphasis on practical optimism vs cynicism; constant output/testing beats debate/politics.
operating_rules: 412 posts across 10 platforms + 81 handles per day = scale via volume + segmentation, not follower count
Interest media (algorithmic relevance) > social media (follower graph)
Consumer is only judge/jury, not CMO opinion, brand lift studies, or ad awards
Midfunnel first: organic creative validation (500+ views) earns right to paid-media dollars
Creative validates organically BEFORE working media spend; reverse order from traditional model
Post 12-14 pieces/day B2B content to get machine-learning data on what works
Platforms + algorithms + culture (PAC) shift constantly; must monitor weekly (LinkedIn now favors images over video as of talk date)
Views editor role: human who understands platform-algorithm shifts in real-time (YouTube Shorts, LinkedIn, X, Substack)
Shift working:non-working media ratio from 85:15 or 80:20 toward 50:50 as creative validation improves
Stop rewarding media agencies on CPM efficiency; reward on creative effectiveness
Experiential events = production day for social content first; experiential experience is secondary
P&H process (platforms & handles): liberate content from corporate comms bottleneck; get executives on X, podcasts, LinkedIn
Stop debating content in boardrooms; post it, measure algorithm + consumer feedback instead
B2B focus: reach developers, CTOs, CFOs, procurement via niche content on LinkedIn, Substack, Twitter X, Beehive
Create 20-30 consumer segmentations per business unit (gender, race, income, interests), then make content directly for each
Real validation happens organically; then take winning creative lower in funnel with CTA + paid media
Microsoft/Fortune 500 brands still using 1960s TV logic on CMO scorecards (GRPs, impressions) = miss on algorithmic age
Practical optimism (maybe-to-everything framework) > cynicism (default no); optimism not same as delusion
Cynicism tax = deploying perspective of 'no' without effort to investigate 'maybe'; blocks discovery of asymmetric upside
Work ethic + accountability + market feedback = proof; reps prove value, not opinions
Most underpriced marketing behavior today: organic social first (midfunnel), not paid media first

contradictions: GaryVee claims platforms are 'fully aligned' with business objectives (want to keep us on longer = better for our reach), but also warns of 'walled gardens' (Gemini will wall-garden YouTube Shorts content to favor YouTube, not broader distribution). Tension between platform incentive alignment and platform lock-in.

Practical optimism framed as different from delusion, but the line between 'maybe I should invest $15k' and delusional thinking isn't sharply defined in the talk. Acknowledges some people ARE delusional but hard to distinguish in practice until post-hoc analysis.

CMOs/marketers blamed for corporate politics + resistance, but also Gary acknowledges they're often right (following corporate scoring systems, avoiding personal risk). Frames as 'being on wrong side of history' but doesn't address that some conservatism is rational given principal-agent misalignment.
weird_gold: 412 posts/day across 81 handles: the industrial-scale content machine. Not thousands of tweets, but 412 intentional pieces. Implies massive templating/batching operation.
VaynerMedia has 100+ employees just monitoring algorithm shifts. This is treated as routine, not AI/ML research. Implies algorithm-literacy is now core marketing ops hire profile.
Views editor as title: recognition that real-time platform-culture reading is a specialist skill, not something CMOs can delegate or learn in 6-month courses.
The P&H (platforms & handles) process: suggests corporate comms bottleneck is THE blocker, not creative talent. If you unblock handles, you get exponential output.

Experiential events reframed as production days first: inverts the whole B2B event economics. Spend less on 'experience,' more on content capture. Event ROI = content factory, not attendee satisfaction.
Email example from 1997 (100k list, 92% open rate) used as proof-of-concept for organic reach before paid amplification. The principle hasn't changed in 30 years, just platforms.
Cynicism tax frame: repackaging sunk-cost regret as a disease/tax, not a personality trait. Makes it treatable/fixable rather than essential identity.
Practical optimism = 'maybe' mindset. Not yes-at-everything, but refusal to kill options before testing. Framed as work (testing), not faith.

'There's always an underpriced arbitrage in marketing': Procter & Gamble on TV (1960s), Amazon on Google Adwords (2000s), Liquid Death on organic social (2020s). Implies marketing epochs defined by what incumbents ignore.
